html:
The script used to write Khmer, the language of Cambodia. It grew out of a southern Indian script, and the oldest dated inscription in the Khmer language was carved in 611 CE at Angkor Borei in southern Cambodia.

Angkor Borei had been a centre of Funan, the early kingdom of the Mekong delta. In the early centuries CE, scribes there and in Chenla used scripts brought from south India, close to the one used by the Pallavas, for both Sanskrit and Khmer. Over time the letters took a local form.

Under the Khmer Empire the script filled temple walls with inscriptions in both languages, and these are a main source for Angkor's history. Khmer is written left to right, with no spaces between words and consonants stacked in clusters. It is still used for Pali texts in Cambodian Buddhism. In the 13th century the old Khmer letters became the model for the Thai script of Sukhothai, and through that for the Lao script.
